\title{Selection Beats Compression: Memory Decision\\Policies for LLM Agents Under a Bounded Store}

\begin{abstract}
A long-running LLM agent cannot keep every turn of a conversation in its
context window, so a memory layer has to decide what to keep, what to compress,
what to forget and what to recall. Tiered memory systems that make these
decisions are already in use, but the decision policy itself has rarely been
isolated and measured. This paper presents MemGate, an evaluation harness that
places competing memory policies on a common accuracy-per-token frontier. Each
comparison is set up so that only one factor differs between the two arms. We
first show that the accounting normally used in this area, which bounds the
context assembled per query but leaves the store unbounded, charges a
store-everything baseline nothing for retention and therefore settles the
comparison in advance. When the store is also bounded, choosing which turns to
forget is worth $+9.37$ answer-recall points over forgetting oldest-first at
identical storage, fidelity and retrieval (95\% CI $[+5.45, +14.90]$ clustered
by conversation, McNemar $p=2.8\!\times\!10^{-5}$), while compressing an evicted
turn instead of dropping it loses $7.13$ points. We also test the
rate--distortion prediction that compression must eventually win. Up to a
compression ratio of $182\times$ it does not, although the margin in favour
of selection narrows. Charging the budget for the embedding index, which is
normally left out, reverses the ranking below about 40\,KiB, where a policy
that stores no index at all performs best. Finally, an LLM-judged salience
scorer performs worse than a regular-expression heuristic by $5.87$ points,
with the confidence interval excluding zero, whereas a logistic scorer over
shallow features and a sentence embedding, trained on LoCoMo and on REALTALK
conversations between real people, beats the heuristic by $+14.55$ points on
held-out LoCoMo conversations (95\% CI $[+10.40, +19.70]$). Across store
budgets from 2048 to 16384 tokens its LoCoMo gain stays significant, and on
REALTALK it becomes significant once the store holds about 40\% of a
conversation. Rebuilt in the same harness, with their settings tuned on the
test corpus in their favour, MemGPT-style and Mem0-style memory both lose to
the learned scorer at every budget from 2048 to 16384 tokens. Held out on
BEAM chats of up to ten million tokens it beats retrieval on every corpus
tested, and when whole one-million-token chats are typed into the application
one message at a time it keeps the answer for 51.9\% of questions against
19.2\% for retrieval. Through a fixed local reader over
all 715 answer-recoverable questions, $+6.0$ points of the selection advantage
convert into correct answers (95\% CI $[+3.3, +9.1]$), which is 69\% of the
recall gap in that run. We release the policy as a working chat application
that runs offline on a laptop, and report three measurement errors that
changed our own results, each found by an invariant rather than by inspection.
\end{abstract}

\begin{IEEEkeywords}
large language models, agent memory, context management, retrieval-augmented
generation, rate--distortion, empirical evaluation
\end{IEEEkeywords}
